title: High-frequency sampling of PFAS at two chemically enhanced primary treatment plants: source-dependent occurrence and diurnal loads
content: Most knowledge of PFASs in wastewater treatment comes from plants with a biological stage, where precursor biotransformation can increase effluent PFCA concentrations above the influent. How incoming wastewater composition shapes PFAS occurrence and its variation through the day remains poorly resolved. This study sampled the influent and effluent at 1–2 h resolution across three complete diurnal cycles at each of the two Norwegian full-scale plants using chemically enhanced primary treatment, one receiving mixed industrial–domestic wastewater (A) and the other domestic wastewater (B). Neither plant has a biological stage, so influent–effluent differences are not confounded by in-plant precursor biotransformation. 14 of 31 target analytes were detected, with short-chain PFCAs, principally PFPeA, dominating both matrices. Median ∑PFAS was 36.5 and 30.3 ng L−1 in the influent and effluent, respectively, at A, and 20.7 and 14.2 ng L−1, respectively, at B. Influent detection frequencies were >87% at A and 5–100% at B, indicating continuous input at A and intermittent inputs at B. Median effluent concentrations did not exceed those of influent at either plant, unlike the increases often reported for activated-sludge systems. Generalized additive models fitted to flow-normalized influent mass loads were consistent with this contrast: B displayed a pronounced diurnal cycle peaking at 11:00–12:00 with a minimum at 05:00–06:00 and a 2.3-fold peak-to-trough amplitude, whereas A showed no significant rhythm, consistent with a continuous industrial baseline masking the domestic signal. These differences suggest that wastewater source composition shapes both the PFAS profile received and its variation over the day, and with it the sampling strategy needed to quantify loads.
